# Signal examples: time and frequency

*Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`timeseries.kt`](reference/math.md#timeseries-kt) for the time-domain filters and detectors, [`spectral.kt`](reference/math.md#spectral-kt) for the frequency-domain half. Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).*

Signal processing needs pictures. A filter can reveal structure or erase the detail you cared about. An event detector can catch a gesture or promote a random spike. The first two examples here work sample by sample in the time domain and keep the raw stream and the processed stream in the same frame; the rest of the page asks what a signal is *made of*, in frequency.

## Filter chains as layered curves

Stacking three filters is easy; seeing whether the stack helped is not. What you want from a smoothing chain is less junk and the same gesture, and those two are traded against each other.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/timeseries_examples/filter_chains.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
val raw = mutableListOf<Float>()
val smooth = mutableListOf<Float>()
val filtered = mutableListOf<Float>()

val ema = EMAFilter(alpha = 0.08f)
val oneEuro = OneEuroFilter(minCutoff = 1.0f, beta = 0.02f, sampleRate = 120f)
val band = BandPassFilter(frequency = 5f, sampleRate = 120f, q = 0.8f)

for (i in 0 until 420) {
    val t = i / 120f
    val signal = (
        sin(2.0 * PI * 1.2 * t).toFloat() * 0.7f +
        sin(2.0 * PI * 4.7 * t + 0.3).toFloat() * 0.22f +
        (-0.12f + random().toFloat() * 0.24f)
    )
    raw += signal
    val s = oneEuro(ema(signal))
    smooth += s
    filtered += band(s)
}

// One call puts all three streams on one axis — raw, the smoothed chain, and the band-passed
// component each get their own trace (dark theme + cyan/orange palette applied).
showSignals(
    "raw" to raw,
    "EMA + One-Euro (smoothed)" to smooth,
    "band-pass (5 Hz)" to filtered,
    channel = "main",
    xTitle = "sample",
)
```

One `showSignals` call puts all three streams on one axis. Watch the chain order: `band` is applied to `s`, the output of `ema` and `oneEuro`, not to `signal`, so the band-pass sees a stream the two smoothers have already been through.

![Three traces over 420 samples: a jagged blue raw signal swinging between +1 and -1, a smooth orange trace at about half that height and some fifteen samples behind it, and a green band-pass trace swinging gently around zero at the same slow rate](assets/timeseries_examples/filter_chains.png)

That order is why the band-pass trace is small and slow: the smoothers upstream removed most of the 4.7 Hz content it is tuned for, so what gets through is a little of the slower 1.2 Hz swing. `BandPassFilter` and `OneEuroFilter` both take `sampleRate = 120f`, so their cutoffs in Hz are right for stored data pushed through in a loop.

## Distribution-aware event flags

Event detectors answer a different question from the filters above: did something noteworthy happen? Both of these fit a distribution to the last `windowSize` samples and fire when the newest one lands in a tail, so nothing fires at all until the window has filled: 64 samples of the 360 here.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/timeseries_examples/distribution_events.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
val gammaEvents = GammaEventDetector(windowSize = 64, tailProbabilityThreshold = 0.03f, influence = 0.15f)
val betaEvents = BetaEventDetector(windowSize = 64, supportMin = -1f, supportMax = 1f, lowerTailThreshold = 0.04f, upperTailThreshold = 0.04f)

val raw = mutableListOf<Float>()
val eg = mutableListOf<Float>()
val eb = mutableListOf<Float>()

for (i in 0 until 360) {
    val t = i / 120f
    var x = (sin(2.0 * PI * 1.1 * t) * 0.55 + (-0.08 + random() * 0.16)).toFloat()
    if (i % 83 == 0) x += 0.95f
    if (i % 127 == 0) x -= 0.8f
    raw += x
    eg += gammaEvents(kotlin.math.abs(x))
    eb += betaEvents(x)
}

// The raw stream and both detectors' verdicts on one axis — the event traces flag their tail
// crossings (beta fires either way, ±1) over the raw motion, so which departures triggered is clear.
showSignals(
    "raw" to raw,
    "gamma events" to eg,
    "beta events" to eb,
    channel = "main",
    xTitle = "sample",
)
```

The stream gets a `+0.95` spike at every 83rd sample and a `-0.8` dip at every 127th, and both detectors report their verdict on the same axis as the signal: `1f` from the gamma detector on the sample that fired, and from the beta detector `+1f` for an upper-tail event and `-1f` for a lower-tail one.

![Three traces over 360 samples: a blue raw signal riding a slow sine, an orange gamma-event trace that spikes to 1 on single samples, and a green beta-event trace that holds at +1 or -1 across long stretches](assets/timeseries_examples/distribution_events.png)

The gamma detector, fed `abs(x)`, marks single samples. The beta detector holds `+1` and `-1` across whole stretches instead, and its window is why: 64 samples is shorter than the 109 the 1.1 Hz sine takes to come round at 120 samples a second, so every fit is a fit over a trend and the trend's own continuation keeps landing in a tail. Give a distribution fit at least one full cycle of any periodic component, or detrend before the detector sees it.

For inline diagnostics of similar live values, continue with [Visualizers](visualizers.md). When the value you care about is *hidden* behind the noise rather than merely buried in it, a state you can only measure indirectly, reach for [State estimation](state_estimation_examples.md).

## From time to frequency

Sometimes the question is what a signal is *made of*: which frequencies carry the energy, how
bright the timbre is, where a chirp is heading. For that Field has an FFT, a windowed `Spectrum`,
a `Spectrogram` (a short-time FFT, or STFT), the usual spectral features, and a resonator bank,
which measures energy at frequencies you choose without running a transform at all. Any length
of signal can be transformed, not just powers of two, and nothing needs an external library or a
GPU.

Each example below synthesises its own signal, analyses it, and draws the result into the box's
output.

## One spectrum

Synthesise a rising chirp plus two steady tones, run a Hann-windowed FFT, and read the shape back
out. `fft(...)` returns a `Spectrum` that knows its sample rate, so bins map to real Hz and the
feature helpers return frequencies you can label.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/one_spectrum.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
// Synthesise a rising linear chirp + two steady tones, FFT it, draw the one-sided spectrum.
val sampleRate = 8000.0
val n = 2048
val f0 = 300.0; val f1 = 3000.0
val dur = n / sampleRate
val k = (f1 - f0) / dur
val signal = DoubleArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate
    // Rising linear chirp (phase-integrated so instantaneous freq sweeps cleanly) + two tones.
    0.9 * sin(2.0 * PI * (f0 * t + 0.5 * k * t * t)) +
        0.4 * sin(2.0 * PI * 700.0 * t) +
        0.3 * sin(2.0 * PI * 1800.0 * t)
}

val spec = fft(signal, WindowType.HANN, sampleRate)
val mag = spec.magnitudeOneSided()   // bins 0 .. N/2
val freqs = spec.frequencies()       // bin -> Hz
val centroid = spec.centroid()       // magnitude-weighted mean frequency, Hz
val rolloff = spec.rolloff(0.85)     // freq below which 85% of the energy sits
val peak = spec.peakFrequency()      // dominant component, Hz

// One call puts the magnitude curve on screen against real Hz, with the centroid and 85% rolloff
// marked as dashed reference lines. showSignals(...) applies the dark theme + cyan/orange palette.
showSignals(
    "magnitude" to mag.toList(),
    x = freqs.toList(),
    channel = "main",
    xTitle = "frequency (Hz)", yTitle = "magnitude",
    marks = [
        "centroid ${"%.0f".format(centroid)} Hz" to centroid,
        "85% rolloff ${"%.0f".format(rolloff)} Hz" to rolloff,
    ],
)
println("peak=${"%.0f".format(peak)}Hz centroid=${"%.0f".format(centroid)}Hz rolloff=${"%.0f".format(rolloff)}Hz bins=${mag.size}")
```

![a cyan magnitude curve on a dark plot, frequency in Hz along the bottom out to 4000 and magnitude up the side to 400. A very narrow spike just under 700 Hz reaches almost the top of the frame; a broad low hump peaks around 70 near 1700 Hz, with a second narrow spike at about 1800 Hz standing on its right shoulder at roughly three-fifths the tall spike's height. Two dashed yellow verticals cross the whole plot, labelled in the legend as the centroid at 1621 Hz and the 85% rolloff at 2172 Hz, and both sit to the right of the tall spike](assets/spectral_examples/one_spectrum.png)

The tall spike is the steady 700 Hz tone, the broad hump is the chirp's energy spread across the
frequencies it swept, and the dashed lines mark the spectral centroid and the 85% rolloff.

## A spectrogram of a chirp

A single spectrum is one slice. An STFT frames the signal, windows each frame, hops forward, and
transforms — giving you a spectrogram: a time × frequency heatmap. The rising chirp becomes a
diagonal ridge, the steady tones stay as horizontal lines, and the per-frame **spectral centroid**
draws a bright trace climbing with the chirp. `showHeatmap(...)` draws the `[frame][bin]` matrix
through a colormap, low frequencies at the bottom, into the box's output.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/spectrogram.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
// --- signal: a rising linear chirp (300 -> 3000 Hz) plus two steady tones (700, 1800 Hz) ---
val sampleRate = 8000.0
val n = 24000                    // 3 s
val f0 = 300.0; val f1 = 3000.0
val dur = n / sampleRate
val k = (f1 - f0) / dur
val signal = DoubleArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate
    // Phase-integrated chirp so the instantaneous frequency f0 + k*t sweeps cleanly below Nyquist.
    0.9 * sin(2.0 * PI * (f0 * t + 0.5 * k * t * t)) +
        0.35 * sin(2.0 * PI * 700.0 * t) +
        0.30 * sin(2.0 * PI * 1800.0 * t)
}

// --- STFT -> magnitude heatmap + spectral-centroid trace ---
val spec = stft(signal, fftSize = 1024, hopSize = 256, window = WindowType.HANN, sampleRate = sampleRate)
val mags = spec.magnitudes()                       // [frame][bin]
val maxMag = spec.maxMagnitude().coerceAtLeast(1e-9)
val centroid = spec.centroidTrace()                // Hz per frame
val nyquist = sampleRate / 2.0

// dB relative to the peak (a useful dynamic range), as a [frame][bin] matrix.
val dB = Array(spec.numFrames) { f ->
    DoubleArray(spec.numBins) { b -> 20.0 * log10((mags[f][b] / maxMag).coerceAtLeast(1e-4)) }
}
// The spectral centroid as a normalized (x, y) overlay: x = time fraction, y = fraction of Nyquist.
val trace = centroid.indices.map { f ->
    (f.toDouble() / (spec.numFrames - 1).coerceAtLeast(1)) to (centroid[f] / nyquist).coerceIn(0.0, 1.0)
}

println("frames=${spec.numFrames} bins=${spec.numBins} centroid ${"%.0f".format(centroid.first())} -> ${"%.0f".format(centroid.last())} Hz")
// One showHeatmap call: transpose [frame][bin] to time × frequency, low frequency at the bottom
// (flipY), the house cyan→orange ramp over a [-80, 0] dB range, with the centroid as a bright overlay.
showHeatmap(dB, colormap = "cyanorange", width = 1800, height = 840, vmin = -80.0, vmax = 0.0,
    transpose = true, flipY = true, overlay = trace, overlayThickness = 3)
```

![a dark time-by-frequency heatmap with low frequency at the bottom. One orange band with a cyan halo runs straight from the bottom-left corner to the top-right; two more lie flat across the full width, the lower about a third of the way up and the other near the middle. A thin white line climbs from the left edge, follows the diagonal for a while, and kinks downward in the last tenth of the frame](assets/spectral_examples/spectrogram.png)

The diagonal ridge is the chirp, the two flat lines are the 700 Hz and 1800 Hz tones, and the thin
trace is the centroid climbing with the sweep. The STFT produces the `[frame][bin]` magnitudes; one
`showHeatmap` call renders them (cyan→orange over a `[-80, 0]` dB range) and draws the centroid
`overlay`.

## Mel bands — a perceptual, log-frequency view

An FFT's bins are evenly spaced in Hz, so most of them land in the upper octaves, where a fixed
number of Hz is a smaller and smaller musical interval.
The **mel scale** warps frequency logarithmically; `Mel.filterBank(...)` collapses a magnitude
spectrum into a handful of triangular mel bands. Applied per STFT frame it gives a mel-spectrogram.
Here the signal is **two crossing chirps** — one rising, one falling — so they trace an X, curved by
the log warping.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/mel_spectrogram.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
// --- signal: two crossing chirps, one rising (200 -> 3200 Hz) and one falling (3200 -> 200 Hz) ---
val sampleRate = 8000.0
val n = 24000
val up0 = 200.0; val up1 = 3200.0
val dn0 = 3200.0; val dn1 = 200.0
val dur = n / sampleRate
val ku = (up1 - up0) / dur
val kd = (dn1 - dn0) / dur
val signal = DoubleArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate
    0.7 * sin(2.0 * PI * (up0 * t + 0.5 * ku * t * t)) +
        0.7 * sin(2.0 * PI * (dn0 * t + 0.5 * kd * t * t))
}

// --- STFT -> per-frame mel filter bank -> heatmap ---
val spec = stft(signal, fftSize = 1024, hopSize = 256, window = WindowType.HANN, sampleRate = sampleRate)
val numBands = 48
val mel = Array(spec.numFrames) { Mel.filterBank(spec.magnitude(it), sampleRate, numBands, 0.0, sampleRate / 2.0) }
var maxMel = 1e-9
for (row in mel) for (v in row) if (v > maxMel) maxMel = v

// dB relative to the peak, as a [frame][band] matrix.
val dB = Array(spec.numFrames) { f ->
    DoubleArray(numBands) { b -> 20.0 * log10((mel[f][b] / maxMel).coerceAtLeast(1e-4)) }
}

println("frames=${spec.numFrames} bands=$numBands")
// transpose [frame][band] to time × mel-band, low band at the bottom.
showHeatmap(dB, colormap = "cyanorange", width = 1800, height = 720, vmin = -80.0, vmax = 0.0,
    transpose = true, flipY = true)
```

![a dark time-by-mel-band heatmap holding two orange bands with cyan halos that cross in a wide X near the middle of the frame. Both are noticeably curved rather than straight, and both are widest where they cross, because the mel bands are broad at the top and narrow at the bottom](assets/spectral_examples/mel_spectrogram.png)

## A resonator bank — frequency analysis without a transform

An FFT frames the signal and asks *all* frequencies at once, on a fixed linear grid set by the
transform size. A **resonator bank** turns that around: run the signal through a set of complex
one-pole resonators, each tuned to a frequency you pick, and each resonator's running magnitude is
the energy near its frequency. There is no window and no frame blocking; it is a per-sample IIR
filterbank, so it streams. Choosing the frequencies yourself also means you can space them
logarithmically (like the ear) and give each its own time constant. `resonate(...)` runs a fixed
bank offline and hands back the per-hop complex output; `resonatorAlphaHeuristics(...)` computes a
smoothing coefficient per frequency, so high resonators settle faster than low ones.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/resonator_bank.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
import afield.audio.engine.resonate
import afield.audio.engine.resonatorAlphaHeuristics

// --- same rising chirp (300 -> 3000 Hz) + two tones (700, 1800 Hz), as a Float signal ---
val sampleRate = 8000f
val n = 24000
val f0 = 300.0; val f1 = 3000.0
val durS = n / sampleRate.toDouble()
val k = (f1 - f0) / durS
val signal = FloatArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate.toDouble()
    (0.9 * sin(2.0 * PI * (f0 * t + 0.5 * k * t * t)) +
        0.35 * sin(2.0 * PI * 700.0 * t) +
        0.30 * sin(2.0 * PI * 1800.0 * t)).toFloat()
}

// --- a bank of complex resonators, log-spaced from 120 Hz to 3900 Hz ---
val numRes = 96
val minHz = 120.0; val maxHz = 3900.0
val freqs = FloatArray(numRes) { i ->
    kotlin.math.exp(ln(minHz) + (ln(maxHz) - ln(minHz)) * i / (numRes - 1)).toFloat()
}
val alphas = resonatorAlphaHeuristics(freqs, sampleRate)  // per-frequency smoothing / time constant
val hop = 256

// resonate returns, per hop slice: numRes real parts then numRes imag parts.
val flat = resonate(signal, sampleRate, freqs, alphas, betas = alphas, hopLength = hop)
val slices = flat.size / (2 * numRes)
fun ampAt(s: Int, kk: Int): Float {
    val base = s * 2 * numRes
    val re = flat[base + kk]; val im = flat[base + numRes + kk]
    return kotlin.math.sqrt(re * re + im * im)
}
var maxA = 1e-9f
for (s in 0 until slices) for (kk in 0 until numRes) { val a = ampAt(s, kk); if (a > maxA) maxA = a }

// dB relative to the peak, as a [slice][resonator] matrix.
val dB = Array(slices) { s ->
    DoubleArray(numRes) { kk -> 20.0 * log10((ampAt(s, kk).toDouble() / maxA).coerceAtLeast(1e-4)) }
}

println("resonators=$numRes slices=$slices freq ${freqs.first().toInt()} -> ${freqs.last().toInt()} Hz")
// transpose [slice][resonator] to time × resonator, low (low-Hz) resonator at the bottom.
showHeatmap(dB, colormap = "cyanorange", width = 1800, height = 720, vmin = -80.0, vmax = 0.0,
    transpose = true, flipY = true)
```

![a time-by-resonator heatmap that is bright cyan almost everywhere, with an orange band rising steeply out of the bottom-left corner and flattening off across the top right, and two more orange bands lying flat across the full width close together near the top. Dark vertical streaks hang down through the lower half](assets/spectral_examples/resonator_bank.png)

Same chirp ridge and two tone lines as the STFT view, but now on a **log-frequency** axis (the tones
sit closer together up top) and with each band carrying its own time constant instead of one shared
window. Because the bank is recursive and per-sample it also runs live as a streaming analyzer.
`TrackingResonatorBank` goes further: each resonator estimates the phase drift of its own output and
retunes towards the instantaneous frequency whenever its local power clears a dynamic threshold,
falling back to its natural frequency when the partial goes away.

## Streaming features that compose with the filter chain

The spectral features also come as `FloatFilter`s, so they slot straight into the same `then`
chain as the [time-domain filters](#filter-chains-as-layered-curves). Feed one sample in, get the latest
feature out (held between hops). Here a rising chirp plus a couple of onsets drives three features at
once, and the three traces are drawn stacked in the box's output.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/streaming_features.png" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
// --- an input stream: a rising chirp (200 -> 2000 Hz) + a steady tone, with two onset bursts ---
val sampleRate = 8000f
val n = 8000                     // 1 s
val stream = FloatArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate
    val f = 200f + 1800f * (i.toFloat() / n)     // sweep 200 -> 2000 Hz
    var s = 0.6f * sin(2.0 * PI * f * t).toFloat() + 0.25f * sin(2.0 * PI * 900.0 * t).toFloat()
    if (i == n / 3 || i == 2 * n / 3) s += 2.0f   // two sharp onsets for the flux detector
    s
}

// The same `then` chain as the time-domain toolkit: smooth the centroid, track flux and level.
val brightness = EMAFilter(0.1f) then SpectralCentroidFilter(fftSize = 1024, hopSize = 256, sampleRate = sampleRate)
val onset = SpectralFluxFilter(fftSize = 1024, hopSize = 256, sampleRate = sampleRate)
val level = RmsFilter(windowSize = 512)

val cTrace = FloatArray(n); val fTrace = FloatArray(n); val rTrace = FloatArray(n)
for (i in 0 until n) {
    cTrace[i] = brightness(stream[i])   // spectral centroid, Hz
    fTrace[i] = onset(stream[i])        // spectral flux (onset novelty)
    rTrace[i] = level(stream[i])        // rolling RMS
}

// The three features live on very different scales (Hz vs flux vs a 0..1 level), so normalize each
// to compare their shape. One call stacks all three; dark theme + cyan/orange palette applied.
showSignals(
    "spectral centroid (Hz)" to cTrace.toList(),
    "spectral flux (onset novelty)" to fTrace.toList(),
    "rolling RMS (level)" to rTrace.toList(),
    channel = "main",
    xTitle = "sample", normalize = true,
)
println("centroid ${"%.0f".format(cTrace[3000])} -> ${"%.0f".format(cTrace[n - 200])} Hz, flux peak ${"%.3f".format(fTrace.maxOrNull() ?: 0f)}")
```

![three normalized traces against sample number on a dark plot. The blue centroid climbs as a staircase from zero to about 0.7 over the first two-thirds, dips, and then steps up to the top of the frame at the right-hand edge. The orange flux sits flat on zero for the first thousand samples, jumps to about 0.92, and stays within a few percent of that for the rest of the run. The green RMS starts at the top, falls at once to about 0.87, and stays there, wobbling slightly](assets/spectral_examples/streaming_features.png)

The smoothed centroid climbs with the chirp and the RMS tracks the overall level. The flux steps up
as soon as its first window fills and then holds near the top of its range: each injected onset is a
step of a percent or two above that plateau, not a spike, because all three traces are normalized to
`0 … 1` for comparison and the flux never returns to its floor once the signal starts.
`SpectralCentroidFilter`, `SpectralRolloffFilter`, `SpectralFluxFilter`, and
`RmsFilter` all maintain their own ring buffer and recompute on each hop, so they behave like any
other per-sample filter in the toolkit.

## What else is in the family

- **FFT** — `fft(...)` / `ifft(...)` over `DoubleArray`, `FloatArray`, or `List<Float>`; forward and
  inverse; power-of-two (radix-2) or arbitrary length (Bluestein).
- **Windows** — `WindowType.RECTANGULAR / HANN / HAMMING / BLACKMAN`, via `Windows.make(...)`.
- **`Spectrum`** — magnitude / power / phase / dB, `binFrequency`, `peakFrequency`, and the feature
  shortcuts `centroid()`, `spread()`, `rolloff()`, `flatness()`.
- **`Spectrogram`** — `stft(...)`, `magnitudes()`, `centroidTrace()` / `rolloffTrace()` /
  `fluxTrace()`, plus `istft(...)` for overlap-add reconstruction back to a signal.
- **Features** — `SpectralFeatures.centroid / spread / rolloff / flux / flatness / rms / energy`.
- **Mel** — `Mel.hzToMel`, `Mel.melToHz`, and a triangular `Mel.filterBank(...)` for perceptual /
  log-frequency band energies.
- **Resonator bank** (`afield.audio.engine`) — `resonate(...)` / `ResonatorBank` for a fixed complex
  filterbank at frequencies you choose, `trackingResonate(...)` / `TrackingResonatorBank` for
  resonators that lock onto and follow moving partials, with `resonatorAlphaHeuristics(...)` for
  per-frequency time constants.

## Filter chains as layered curves

Stacking three filters is easy; seeing whether the stack helped is not. What you want from a smoothing chain is less junk and the same gesture, and those two are traded against each other.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/timeseries_examples/filter_chains.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
val raw = mutableListOf<Float>()
val smooth = mutableListOf<Float>()
val filtered = mutableListOf<Float>()

val ema = EMAFilter(alpha = 0.08f)

val band = BandPassFilter(frequency = 5f, sampleRate = 120f, q = 0.8f)

for (i in 0 until 420) {
    val t = i / 120f

        sin(2.0 * PI * 1.2 * t).toFloat() * 0.7f +
        sin(2.0 * PI * 4.7 * t + 0.3).toFloat() * 0.22f +
        (-0.12f + random().toFloat() * 0.24f)
    )
    raw += signal
    val s = oneEuro(ema(signal))
    smooth += s
    filtered += band(s)
}

// One call puts all three streams on one axis — raw, the smoothed chain, and the band-passed
// component each get their own trace (dark theme + cyan/orange palette applied).

    "raw" to raw,
    "EMA + One-Euro (smoothed)" to smooth,
    "band-pass (5 Hz)" to filtered,

```

One `showSignals` call puts all three streams on one axis. Watch the chain order: `band` is applied to `s`, the output of `ema` and `oneEuro`, not to `signal`, so the band-pass sees a stream the two smoothers have already been through.

That order is why the band-pass trace is small and slow: the smoothers upstream removed most of the 4.7 Hz content it is tuned for, so what gets through is a little of the slower 1.2 Hz swing. `BandPassFilter` and `OneEuroFilter` both take `sampleRate = 120f`, so their cutoffs in Hz are right for stored data pushed through in a loop.

## Distribution-aware event flags

Event detectors answer a different question from the filters above: did something noteworthy happen? Both of these fit a distribution to the last `windowSize` samples and fire when the newest one lands in a tail, so nothing fires at all until the window has filled: 64 samples of the 360 here.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/timeseries_examples/distribution_events.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
val gammaEvents = GammaEventDetector(windowSize = 64, tailProbabilityThreshold = 0.03f, influence = 0.15f)
val betaEvents = BetaEventDetector(windowSize = 64, supportMin = -1f, supportMax = 1f, lowerTailThreshold = 0.04f, upperTailThreshold = 0.04f)

val raw = mutableListOf<Float>()
val eg = mutableListOf<Float>()
val eb = mutableListOf<Float>()

for (i in 0 until 360) {
    val t = i / 120f
    var x = (sin(2.0 * PI * 1.1 * t) * 0.55 + (-0.08 + random() * 0.16)).toFloat()
    if (i % 83 == 0) x += 0.95f
    if (i % 127 == 0) x -= 0.8f
    raw += x
    eg += gammaEvents(kotlin.math.abs(x))
    eb += betaEvents(x)
}

// The raw stream and both detectors' verdicts on one axis — the event traces flag their tail
// crossings (beta fires either way, ±1) over the raw motion, so which departures triggered is clear.
showSignals(
    "raw" to raw,
    "gamma events" to eg,
    "beta events" to eb,
    channel = "main",
    xTitle = "sample",
)
```

The stream gets a `+0.95` spike at every 83rd sample and a `-0.8` dip at every 127th, and both detectors report their verdict on the same axis as the signal: `1f` from the gamma detector on the sample that fired, and from the beta detector `+1f` for an upper-tail event and `-1f` for a lower-tail one.

![Three traces over 360 samples: a blue raw signal riding a slow sine, an orange gamma-event trace that spikes to 1 on single samples, and a green beta-event trace that holds at +1 or -1 across long stretches](assets/timeseries_examples/distribution_events.png)

The gamma detector, fed `abs(x)`, marks single samples. The beta detector holds `+1` and `-1` across whole stretches instead, and its window is why: 64 samples is shorter than the 109 the 1.1 Hz sine takes to come round at 120 samples a second, so every fit is a fit over a trend and the trend's own continuation keeps landing in a tail. Give a distribution fit at least one full cycle of any periodic component, or detrend before the detector sees it.

For inline diagnostics of similar live values, continue with [Visualizers](visualizers.md). When the value you care about is *hidden* behind the noise rather than merely buried in it, a state you can only measure indirectly, reach for [State estimation](state_estimation_examples.md).

## From time to frequency

Sometimes the question is what a signal is *made of*: which frequencies carry the energy, how
bright the timbre is, where a chirp is heading. For that Field has an FFT, a windowed `Spectrum`,
a `Spectrogram` (a short-time FFT, or STFT), the usual spectral features, and a resonator bank,
which measures energy at frequencies you choose without running a transform at all. Any length
of signal can be transformed, not just powers of two, and nothing needs an external library or a
GPU.

Each example below synthesises its own signal, analyses it, and draws the result into the box's
output.

## One spectrum

Synthesise a rising chirp plus two steady tones, run a Hann-windowed FFT, and read the shape back
out. `fft(...)` returns a `Spectrum` that knows its sample rate, so bins map to real Hz and the
feature helpers return frequencies you can label.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/one_spectrum.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}

val n = 2048
val f0 = 300.0; val f1 = 3000.0
val dur = n / sampleRate
val k = (f1 - f0) / dur
val signal = DoubleArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate
    // Rising linear chirp (phase-integrated so instantaneous freq sweeps cleanly) + two tones.
    0.9 * sin(2.0 * PI * (f0 * t + 0.5 * k * t * t)) +
        0.4 * sin(2.0 * PI * 700.0 * t) +
        0.3 * sin(2.0 * PI * 1800.0 * t)
}

val rolloff = spec.rolloff(0.85)     // freq below which 85% of the energy sits
val peak = spec.peakFrequency()      // dominant component, Hz

// One call puts the magnitude curve on screen against real Hz, with the centroid and 85% rolloff
// marked as dashed reference lines. showSignals(...) applies the dark theme + cyan/orange palette.

    "magnitude" to mag.toList(),
    x = freqs.toList(),
    channel = "main",
    xTitle = "frequency (Hz)", yTitle = "magnitude",
    marks = [

        "85% rolloff ${"%.0f".format(rolloff)} Hz" to rolloff,
    ],
)
println("peak=${"%.0f".format(peak)}Hz centroid=${"%.0f".format(centroid)}Hz rolloff=${"%.0f".format(rolloff)}Hz bins=${mag.size}")
```

## A spectrogram of a chirp

A single spectrum is one slice. An STFT frames the signal, windows each frame, hops forward, and
transforms — giving you a spectrogram: a time × frequency heatmap. The rising chirp becomes a
diagonal ridge, the steady tones stay as horizontal lines, and the per-frame **spectral centroid**
draws a bright trace climbing with the chirp. `showHeatmap(...)` draws the `[frame][bin]` matrix
through a colormap, low frequencies at the bottom, into the box's output.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/spectrogram.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
// --- signal: a rising linear chirp (300 -> 3000 Hz) plus two steady tones (700, 1800 Hz) ---
val sampleRate = 8000.0
val n = 24000                    // 3 s
val f0 = 300.0; val f1 = 3000.0
val dur = n / sampleRate
val k = (f1 - f0) / dur
val signal = DoubleArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate
    // Phase-integrated chirp so the instantaneous frequency f0 + k*t sweeps cleanly below Nyquist.
    0.9 * sin(2.0 * PI * (f0 * t + 0.5 * k * t * t)) +
        0.35 * sin(2.0 * PI * 700.0 * t) +
        0.30 * sin(2.0 * PI * 1800.0 * t)
}

// --- STFT -> magnitude heatmap + spectral-centroid trace ---
val spec = stft(signal, fftSize = 1024, hopSize = 256, window = WindowType.HANN, sampleRate = sampleRate)
val mags = spec.magnitudes()                       // [frame][bin]
val maxMag = spec.maxMagnitude().coerceAtLeast(1e-9)
val centroid = spec.centroidTrace()                // Hz per frame
val nyquist = sampleRate / 2.0

// dB relative to the peak (a useful dynamic range), as a [frame][bin] matrix.
val dB = Array(spec.numFrames) { f ->
    DoubleArray(spec.numBins) { b -> 20.0 * log10((mags[f][b] / maxMag).coerceAtLeast(1e-4)) }
}
// The spectral centroid as a normalized (x, y) overlay: x = time fraction, y = fraction of Nyquist.
val trace = centroid.indices.map { f ->
    (f.toDouble() / (spec.numFrames - 1).coerceAtLeast(1)) to (centroid[f] / nyquist).coerceIn(0.0, 1.0)
}

println("frames=${spec.numFrames} bins=${spec.numBins} centroid ${"%.0f".format(centroid.first())} -> ${"%.0f".format(centroid.last())} Hz")
// One showHeatmap call: transpose [frame][bin] to time × frequency, low frequency at the bottom
// (flipY), the house cyan→orange ramp over a [-80, 0] dB range, with the centroid as a bright overlay.
showHeatmap(dB, colormap = "cyanorange", width = 1800, height = 840, vmin = -80.0, vmax = 0.0,
    transpose = true, flipY = true, overlay = trace, overlayThickness = 3)
```

## Mel bands — a perceptual, log-frequency view

An FFT's bins are evenly spaced in Hz, so most of them land in the upper octaves, where a fixed
number of Hz is a smaller and smaller musical interval.
The **mel scale** warps frequency logarithmically; `Mel.filterBank(...)` collapses a magnitude
spectrum into a handful of triangular mel bands. Applied per STFT frame it gives a mel-spectrogram.
Here the signal is **two crossing chirps** — one rising, one falling — so they trace an X, curved by
the log warping.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/mel_spectrogram.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
// --- signal: two crossing chirps, one rising (200 -> 3200 Hz) and one falling (3200 -> 200 Hz) ---
val sampleRate = 8000.0
val n = 24000
val up0 = 200.0; val up1 = 3200.0
val dn0 = 3200.0; val dn1 = 200.0
val dur = n / sampleRate
val ku = (up1 - up0) / dur
val kd = (dn1 - dn0) / dur
val signal = DoubleArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate
    0.7 * sin(2.0 * PI * (up0 * t + 0.5 * ku * t * t)) +
        0.7 * sin(2.0 * PI * (dn0 * t + 0.5 * kd * t * t))
}

// --- STFT -> per-frame mel filter bank -> heatmap ---
val spec = stft(signal, fftSize = 1024, hopSize = 256, window = WindowType.HANN, sampleRate = sampleRate)
val numBands = 48
val mel = Array(spec.numFrames) { Mel.filterBank(spec.magnitude(it), sampleRate, numBands, 0.0, sampleRate / 2.0) }
var maxMel = 1e-9
for (row in mel) for (v in row) if (v > maxMel) maxMel = v

// dB relative to the peak, as a [frame][band] matrix.
val dB = Array(spec.numFrames) { f ->
    DoubleArray(numBands) { b -> 20.0 * log10((mel[f][b] / maxMel).coerceAtLeast(1e-4)) }
}

println("frames=${spec.numFrames} bands=$numBands")
// transpose [frame][band] to time × mel-band, low band at the bottom.
showHeatmap(dB, colormap = "cyanorange", width = 1800, height = 720, vmin = -80.0, vmax = 0.0,
    transpose = true, flipY = true)
```

## A resonator bank — frequency analysis without a transform

An FFT frames the signal and asks *all* frequencies at once, on a fixed linear grid set by the
transform size. A **resonator bank** turns that around: run the signal through a set of complex
one-pole resonators, each tuned to a frequency you pick, and each resonator's running magnitude is
the energy near its frequency. There is no window and no frame blocking; it is a per-sample IIR
filterbank, so it streams. Choosing the frequencies yourself also means you can space them
logarithmically (like the ear) and give each its own time constant. `resonate(...)` runs a fixed
bank offline and hands back the per-hop complex output; `resonatorAlphaHeuristics(...)` computes a
smoothing coefficient per frequency, so high resonators settle faster than low ones.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/resonator_bank.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
import afield.audio.engine.resonate
import afield.audio.engine.resonatorAlphaHeuristics

// --- same rising chirp (300 -> 3000 Hz) + two tones (700, 1800 Hz), as a Float signal ---
val sampleRate = 8000f
val n = 24000
val f0 = 300.0; val f1 = 3000.0
val durS = n / sampleRate.toDouble()
val k = (f1 - f0) / durS
val signal = FloatArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate.toDouble()
    (0.9 * sin(2.0 * PI * (f0 * t + 0.5 * k * t * t)) +
        0.35 * sin(2.0 * PI * 700.0 * t) +
        0.30 * sin(2.0 * PI * 1800.0 * t)).toFloat()
}

// --- a bank of complex resonators, log-spaced from 120 Hz to 3900 Hz ---
val numRes = 96
val minHz = 120.0; val maxHz = 3900.0
val freqs = FloatArray(numRes) { i ->
    kotlin.math.exp(ln(minHz) + (ln(maxHz) - ln(minHz)) * i / (numRes - 1)).toFloat()
}
val alphas = resonatorAlphaHeuristics(freqs, sampleRate)  // per-frequency smoothing / time constant
val hop = 256

// resonate returns, per hop slice: numRes real parts then numRes imag parts.
val flat = resonate(signal, sampleRate, freqs, alphas, betas = alphas, hopLength = hop)
val slices = flat.size / (2 * numRes)
fun ampAt(s: Int, kk: Int): Float {
    val base = s * 2 * numRes
    val re = flat[base + kk]; val im = flat[base + numRes + kk]
    return kotlin.math.sqrt(re * re + im * im)
}
var maxA = 1e-9f
for (s in 0 until slices) for (kk in 0 until numRes) { val a = ampAt(s, kk); if (a > maxA) maxA = a }

// dB relative to the peak, as a [slice][resonator] matrix.
val dB = Array(slices) { s ->
    DoubleArray(numRes) { kk -> 20.0 * log10((ampAt(s, kk).toDouble() / maxA).coerceAtLeast(1e-4)) }
}

println("resonators=$numRes slices=$slices freq ${freqs.first().toInt()} -> ${freqs.last().toInt()} Hz")
// transpose [slice][resonator] to time × resonator, low (low-Hz) resonator at the bottom.
showHeatmap(dB, colormap = "cyanorange", width = 1800, height = 720, vmin = -80.0, vmax = 0.0,
    transpose = true, flipY = true)
```

Dark vertical streaks hang down through the lower half](assets/spectral_examples/resonator_bank.png)

Same chirp ridge and two tone lines as the STFT view, but now on a **log-frequency** axis (the tones
sit closer together up top) and with each band carrying its own time constant instead of one shared
window. Because the bank is recursive and per-sample it also runs live as a streaming analyzer.
`TrackingResonatorBank` goes further: each resonator estimates the phase drift of its own output and
retunes towards the instantaneous frequency whenever its local power clears a dynamic threshold,
falling back to its natural frequency when the partial goes away.

## Streaming features that compose with the filter chain

The spectral features also come as `FloatFilter`s, so they slot straight into the same `then`
chain as the [time-domain filters](#filter-chains-as-layered-curves). Feed one sample in, get the latest
feature out (held between hops). Here a rising chirp plus a couple of onsets drives three features at
once, and the three traces are drawn stacked in the box's output.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/spectral_examples/streaming_features.png" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
// --- an input stream: a rising chirp (200 -> 2000 Hz) + a steady tone, with two onset bursts ---
val sampleRate = 8000f
val n = 8000                     // 1 s
val duration = n / sampleRate.toDouble()
val startHz = 200.0
val endHz = 2000.0
val chirpRate = (endHz - startHz) / duration
val stream = FloatArray(n) { i ->
    val t = i / sampleRate.toDouble()
    // Integrate frequency: the phase derivative is startHz + chirpRate * t.
    val phase = 2.0 * PI * (startHz * t + 0.5 * chirpRate * t * t)
    var s = 0.6f * sin(phase).toFloat() + 0.25f * sin(2.0 * PI * 900.0 * t).toFloat()
    if (i == n / 3 || i == 2 * n / 3) s += 2.0f   // two sharp onsets for the flux detector
    s
}

// The same `then` chain as the time-domain toolkit: smooth the centroid, track flux and level.
val brightness = EMAFilter(0.1f) then SpectralCentroidFilter(fftSize = 1024, hopSize = 256, sampleRate = sampleRate)
val onset = SpectralFluxFilter(fftSize = 1024, hopSize = 256, sampleRate = sampleRate)
val level = RmsFilter(windowSize = 512)

val cTrace = FloatArray(n); val fTrace = FloatArray(n); val rTrace = FloatArray(n)
for (i in 0 until n) {
    cTrace[i] = brightness(stream[i])   // spectral centroid, Hz
    fTrace[i] = onset(stream[i])        // spectral flux (onset novelty)
    rTrace[i] = level(stream[i])        // rolling RMS
}

// The three features live on very different scales (Hz vs flux vs a 0..1 level), so normalize each
// to compare their shape. One call stacks all three; dark theme + cyan/orange palette applied.
showSignals(
    "spectral centroid (Hz)" to cTrace.toList(),
    "spectral flux (onset novelty)" to fTrace.toList(),
    "rolling RMS (level)" to rTrace.toList(),
    channel = "main",
    xTitle = "sample", normalize = true,
)
println("centroid ${"%.0f".format(cTrace[3000])} -> ${"%.0f".format(cTrace[n - 200])} Hz, flux peak ${"%.3f".format(fTrace.maxOrNull() ?: 0f)}")
```

![Normalized streaming features: cyan spectral centroid climbs in steps, orange flux holds a high plateau after the first FFT window, and green RMS stays near its baseline with a broad peak as the chirp passes the steady tone](assets/spectral_examples/streaming_features.png)

The smoothed centroid climbs with the chirp and the RMS tracks the overall level. The flux steps up
as soon as its first window fills and then holds near the top of its range: each injected onset is a
step of a percent or two above that plateau, not a spike, because all three traces are normalized to
`0 … 1` for comparison and the flux never returns to its floor once the signal starts.
`SpectralCentroidFilter`, `SpectralRolloffFilter`, `SpectralFluxFilter`, and
`RmsFilter` all maintain their own ring buffer and recompute on each hop, so they behave like any
other per-sample filter in the toolkit.

## What else is in the family

- **FFT** — `fft(...)` / `ifft(...)` over `DoubleArray`, `FloatArray`, or `List<Float>`; forward and
  inverse; power-of-two (radix-2) or arbitrary length (Bluestein).
- **Windows** — `WindowType.RECTANGULAR / HANN / HAMMING / BLACKMAN`, via `Windows.make(...)`.
- **`Spectrum`** — magnitude / power / phase / dB, `binFrequency`, `peakFrequency`, and the feature
  shortcuts `centroid()`, `spread()`, `rolloff()`, `flatness()`.
- **`Spectrogram`** — `stft(...)`, `magnitudes()`, `centroidTrace()` / `rolloffTrace()` /
  `fluxTrace()`, plus `istft(...)` for overlap-add reconstruction back to a signal.
- **Features** — `SpectralFeatures.centroid / spread / rolloff / flux / flatness / rms / energy`.
- **Mel** — `Mel.hzToMel`, `Mel.melToHz`, and a triangular `Mel.filterBank(...)` for perceptual /
  log-frequency band energies.
- **Resonator bank** (`afield.audio.engine`) — `resonate(...)` / `ResonatorBank` for a fixed complex
  filterbank at frequencies you choose, `trackingResonate(...)` / `TrackingResonatorBank` for
  resonators that lock onto and follow moving partials, with `resonatorAlphaHeuristics(...)` for
  per-frequency time constants.

# Measuring dependence between two signals *Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [Math](reference/math.md) and [Data](reference/data.md).* You have two streams of numbers and want to know whether they are related. Field's tools for that live in `afield/math/statistics/stats.kt`, `afield/math/statistics/correlations.kt` and `afield/math/statistics/quantilewarp.kt` (package `afield.math.statistics`), and this page works through all three. Each dependence coefficient answers a slightly different version of the question, so the page shows which one to use for which kind of relationship. `stats.kt` has the summary statistics: count, quartiles, IQR, MAD, skew, kurtosis, histograms and a streaming window of all of it. `correlations.kt` has the dependence coefficients: Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, Chatterjee's xi, distance correlation, a MIC-like grid scan, and rolling versions of the last two. `quantilewarp.kt` reshapes a signal's *distribution* into one you choose, for when a signal has the wrong shape to work with. ## Where the family lives
| what you want | where it is | notes | |---|---|---| | count, quartiles, IQR, MAD, variance, skew, excess kurtosis | `stats.kt` | `buildSummaryStats` → `SummaryStats`. Non-finite input is dropped *and counted* | | a streaming window of all of that | `stats.kt` | `SummaryStatsBuffer`, plus `Vec2`/`Vec3`/`Vec4SummaryStatsBuffer` which add per-component stats, vector length and the pairwise component correlations | | histograms | `stats.kt` | `buildHistogram` → `Histogram` / `HistogramBin` | | those, rendered | `stats.kt` | `histogramToSvg`, `seriesPlotToSvg`, `summaryStatsBoxToHtml` — string-interpolated SVG/HTML, no drawing library, cyan-on-black by default | | **the dependence coefficients** | `correlations.kt` | `StatsDependence.pearson` / `spearman` / `kendallTauB` / `chatterjeeXi` (aliased `xi`) / `distanceCorrelation` / `micTicNaive` | | dependence over a sliding window | `correlations.kt` | `RollingDistanceCorrelation` (incremental, O(w) per sample), `RollingXiCorrelation` (recomputes, O(w log w) per sample) | | reshape a distribution into a target | `quantilewarp.kt` | `AdaptiveQuantileWarp`, `QuantileWarpState`, `TargetDistributions`, `inverseStandardNormalCdf`, and matching GLSL for the GPU |
There are no p-values, confidence intervals or hypothesis tests in these files. Whether a number means anything is yours to establish, and *Measuring the null yourself* below writes the permutation test that does it. Note too that `micTicNaive` is not MICe/TICe. [Values Over Time](interpolants_examples.md) has a shorter version of the dependence examples, next to the interpolants. ## Summary statistics `buildSummaryStats` takes any `Iterable` and hands back seventeen numbers. `SummaryStatsBuffer` wraps it in a synchronized, capped sliding window you can `add` to sample by sample, and `summaryHtml()` renders the whole thing (metrics, histogram and series plot) as one self-contained HTML card. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/statistics_examples/summary_card.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="760" h="640" padding="16"} :::static // A right-skewed signal by construction: exp of a Gaussian, so we know the shape we are asking about. val rng = java.util.Random(11) val signal = (0 until 500).map { exp(0.6 * rng.nextGaussian()) } val buf = SummaryStatsBuffer(maxSize = 500) buf.addAll(signal) buf.add(Double.NaN) // dropped, and counted, at `add` time buf.add(Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY) // likewise: `values` never holds a non-finite number val s = buf.snapshot() /* Three things the card reports that are easy to misread, pinned here as arithmetic: - MAD is the *median absolute deviation from the median*, unscaled. If you are comparing against another tool, the mapping onto NumPy and SciPy is exact: `q1`/`median`/`q3` are `numpy.percentile`'s default linear interpolation, `mad` is `median(|y − median(y)|)` unscaled, `sampleStdDev` is `numpy.std(ddof=1)`, and `skewness`/`kurtosisExcess` are `scipy.stats.skew` and `scipy.stats.kurtosis` at their *default* `bias=True`. `StatsSummaryTest` pins that mapping to ten decimal places against SciPy 1.15.2 on a tie-heavy ten-point sample. Feed 200 finite samples to a `maxSize = 64` buffer and you get `size=64, samplesSeen=200, droppedByCapacity=136`. ## Histograms, and the rule that picks the bins `buildHistogram` chooses its own bin width: the **smallest** of the Freedman–Diaconis, Scott and Sturges estimates, floored at `range/2000` so the bin count can never exceed 2000. "Smallest" means finest, which is usually what you want. The fence below re-derives the whole decision from the published `SummaryStats` and predicts the bin count before asking. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/statistics_examples/histogram_rule.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1020" h="560" padding="16"} :::static val rng = java.util.Random(11) val skewed = (0 until 500).map { exp(0.6 * rng.nextGaussian()) } // Two clean modes, 4 apart, each with sd 0.4 — the case the rule handles worst. val rng2 = java.util.Random(23) val bimodal = (0 until 500).map { if (it % 2 == 0) -2.0 + 0.4 * rng2.nextGaussian() else 2.0 + 0.4 * rng2.nextGaussian() } /* Re-derive the three candidate widths from the public stats and predict the bin count. This shares `quantileSorted` with the implementation, so it checks the *rule selection and the rounding* — not the quantiles themselves. Those are checked against SciPy in jvmTest instead. */ fun explain(name: String, values: List): String { val s = buildSummaryStats(values) val n = s.count val range = s.max - s.min val cubeRootN = n.toDouble().pow(-1.0 / 3.0) val hFd = 2.0 * s.iqr * cubeRootN // Freedman-Diaconis val hScott = 3.5 * s.sampleStdDev * cubeRootN // Scott val kSturges = ceil(ln(n.toDouble()) / ln(2.0) + 1.0).toInt() // Sturges val hSturges = range / kSturges val winner = minOf(hFd, hScott, hSturges) val which = when (winner) { hFd -> "Freedman-Diaconis" hScott -> "Scott" else -> "Sturges" } val predicted = Math.round(range / winner).toInt().coerceIn(1, 2000) val actual = buildHistogram(values) return "$name: FD=${"%.4f".format(hFd)} Scott=${"%.4f".format(hScott)} " + "Sturges=${"%.4f".format(hSturges)} (k=$kSturges) -> $which wins; " + "predicted ${predicted} bins of ${"%.5f".format(range / predicted)}, " + "got ${actual.bins.size} of ${"%.5f".format(actual.binWidth)}; counts sum to ${actual.count}" } val skewedNote = explain("skewed", skewed) val bimodalNote = explain("bimodal", bimodal) :::fold draw both histograms val svgs = [ histogramToSvg( buildHistogram(skewed), widthPx = 470, heightPx = 270, padTop = 26, title = "exp(0.6 g), n=500", decimals = 3, ), histogramToSvg( buildHistogram(bimodal), widthPx = 470, heightPx = 270, padTop = 26, title = "two modes at -2 and +2, n=500", decimals = 3, ), ] showRow("histograms", svgs) markdown( "the rule, re-derived", """ {muted:$skewedNote} {muted:$bimodalNote} """, width = 960, ) :::endfold ``` ![Two histograms: a right-skewed unimodal signal resolved into 28 bins, and a clean two-mode signal resolved into only 10](assets/statistics_examples/histogram_rule.png) Both predictions land: 28 bins of 0.21431 for the skewed signal, 10 bins of 0.63290 for the bimodal one, and in both cases the bin counts sum back to 500. Which rule won is the part to read. On the skewed signal Freedman–Diaconis is the finest at 0.2162 and it decides. On the bimodal signal FD comes out at **1.0065** and Scott at **0.9077** (both much coarser) because both are driven by global spread, and here the spread is the *distance between* the modes (IQR 3.99, sample sd 2.06) rather than the spread within them (0.4). Which leaves **Sturges** winning at 0.6329, and Sturges is the one rule of the three that looks at nothing but n: `ceil(log₂ n + 1)` is 10 bins for *any* 500-point sample whatever its shape. So a multi-modal signal falls back to the crudest of the three estimates and its two obvious modes get about one bin each. `buildHistogram` takes no bin-count argument (`stats.kt:1214#There is no bin-count parameter`), so if you need finer bins for a signal like this, bin it yourself. ## Comparing the dependence coefficients Every coefficient in `StatsDependence` takes two equal-length `DoubleArray`s and returns one number, but they measure different things. But they side with Pearson on the parabola, and for the same reason: a parabola is a function and not a monotone one, and monotone is all either of them can see. `spearman` is literally `pearson` on `ranksAverageTies` (`correlations.kt:176#is constant, since every rank is then identical and [pearson]`–`correlations.kt:181#val ry = ranksAverageTies(y)`), so it inherits every Pearson limitation *after* the ranking. **Chatterjee's xi answers "is `y` a function of `x`", and it is the only asymmetric coefficient here.** It reads 0.985 on the parabola and 0.955 on the sine, the two cases the rank coefficients miss entirely. Swap the arguments and it changes its mind: `xi(x, parabola) = 0.985` but `xi(parabola, x) = 0.246`, because `x` genuinely is *not* a function of `x²` — each `y` has two possible `x`. Cheap, too: O(n log n) against the O(n²) of `kendallTauB` and `distanceCorrelation`. **Distance correlation answers "is there any dependence at all".** It is the only entry in the table that is non-zero on *every* dependent row, including the last interesting one: the growing-spread panel, where `y` has the same mean everywhere and only its *scale* depends on `x`. Pearson, Spearman and Kendall read 0.00 there. So does xi (0.026), and rightly so: `y` is not a function of `x`, it is a random variable whose spread is. Distance correlation reads 0.193, and the next section puts that against the null it would have to beat. **And the trap in reading distance correlation**: it is *not* a measure of how strong the dependence is. dCor is 1 only for an exactly linear relationship (`distanceCorrelation(x, 3x+1)` is exactly `1.0`, and so is `distanceCorrelation(x, −2x+5)`; it is unsigned). On the parabola, where `y` is a perfect function of `x`, it reads 0.491; on the sine, 0.286. Lower dCor does not mean weaker dependence, it means less *linear* dependence. Use it to decide whether to keep looking, then use something else to describe what you found. ??? note "How `xi` handles a tied predictor" Chatterjee's estimator is only defined up to a *random* breaking of the ties among the `x` values, so on tied `x` it is a random variable rather than a number. Rather than pick a seed, `chatterjeeXi` returns that random variable's **exact expectation**, computed in closed form from the ranks inside each run of equal `x` (`correlations.kt:325#val denominator = 2.0 * denomTerm.toDouble()`–`correlations.kt:353`). So it is deterministic, reproducible, and invariant to the order you hand the pairs over in. Two consequences. A **constant predictor reads 0**: for a single tie group the numerator's expectation is `(n²−1)/3` against a denominator of `n(n²−1)/3`, so the closed form is exactly zero for every `n`. In `Double` it is zero to within one ulp rather than bit-exact, so compare it against a tolerance, not against `0.0`; [`dev_docs/STATISTICS_MEASUREMENTS.md`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/dev_docs/STATISTICS_MEASUREMENTS.md) has the sweep that bound comes from. And a quantised predictor (a bucketed index, an integer control value, a thresholded signal) is answered correctly: heavy ties with a real relationship still read high (a ten-block staircase reads **0.891**), while heavy ties with no relationship read ~0. Inputs whose `x` values are all distinct are unaffected, bit for bit, so every number elsewhere on this page is a tie-free case. Every other coefficient here refuses a constant outright: `pearson`, `spearman` and `kendallTauB` return NaN, and `distanceCorrelation` returns 0.0. ??? aside "Agents: xi values recorded before 2026-07-30" Recorded xi values on tied `x` from before 2026-07-30 are wrong, not merely different: x-ties then broke by input index, which scored how nearly `y` was a function of the order the samples arrived in. That matters most for distance correlation, because dCor under genuine independence is **not** 0 at finite n: the estimator is biased upward, and the bias is large enough to swamp a real effect if you do not know its size. The `independent` row above reads 0.068 at n=400; shrink the sample and the bias grows fast, and by n=25 the null's 95th percentile is up at 0.466. So measure the null yourself. Re-pair `y` against `x` at random a few hundred times, and see where the number you actually observed falls: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/statistics_examples/null_distribution.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="820" padding="16"} :::static val n = 400 val x = DoubleArray(n) { it / (n - 1.0) * 2.0 - 1.0 } val rng = java.util.Random(7) val noise = DoubleArray(n) { rng.nextGaussian() } val y = DoubleArray(n) { (0.05 + abs(x[it])) * noise[it] } // the growing-spread panel again val observedDcor = StatsDependence.distanceCorrelation(x, y) val observedXi = StatsDependence.xi(x, y) // The null: break the pairing, keep both marginals. At n = 50 the threshold is around 0.34, so anything short of a strong relationship is invisible; distance correlation needs a few hundred samples before it can see a subtle one. ## Rolling: finding when the relationship starts A single coefficient over a whole recording answers the wrong question if the relationship comes and goes. `RollingDistanceCorrelation` maintains its row sums, grand sums and cross sums incrementally, so a `push` costs O(w) rather than the O(w²) a rebuild would (`correlations.kt:673#The maintained row sums, grand sums and cross sums are only ever`). `RollingXiCorrelation` makes no such promise. It recomputes `chatterjeeXi` over the window every time, at O(w log w) (`correlations.kt:917#have arrived. Each dependence coefficient answers a slightly different version of the question, so the page shows which one to use for which kind of relationship. `stats.kt` has the summary statistics: count, quartiles, IQR, MAD, skew, kurtosis, histograms and a streaming window of all of it. `correlations.kt` has the dependence coefficients: Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, Chatterjee's xi, distance correlation, a MIC-like grid scan, and rolling versions of the last two. `quantilewarp.kt` reshapes a signal's *distribution* into one you choose, for when a signal has the wrong shape to work with. ## Where the family lives
| what you want | where it is | notes | |---|---|---| | count, quartiles, IQR, MAD, variance, skew, excess kurtosis | `stats.kt` | `buildSummaryStats` → `SummaryStats`. Non-finite input is dropped *and counted* | | a streaming window of all of that | `stats.kt` | `SummaryStatsBuffer`, plus `Vec2`/`Vec3`/`Vec4SummaryStatsBuffer` which add per-component stats, vector length and the pairwise component correlations | | histograms | `stats.kt` | `buildHistogram` → `Histogram` / `HistogramBin` | | those, rendered | `stats.kt` | `histogramToSvg`, `seriesPlotToSvg`, `summaryStatsBoxToHtml` — string-interpolated SVG/HTML, no drawing library, cyan-on-black by default | | **the dependence coefficients** | `correlations.kt` | `StatsDependence.pearson` / `spearman` / `kendallTauB` / `chatterjeeXi` (aliased `xi`) / `distanceCorrelation` / `micTicNaive` | | dependence over a sliding window | `correlations.kt` | `RollingDistanceCorrelation` (incremental, O(w) per sample), `RollingXiCorrelation` (recomputes, O(w log w) per sample) | | reshape a distribution into a target | `quantilewarp.kt` | `AdaptiveQuantileWarp`, `QuantileWarpState`, `TargetDistributions`, `inverseStandardNormalCdf`, and matching GLSL for the GPU |

A **constant predictor reads 0**: for a single tie group the numerator's expectation is `(n²−1)/3` against a denominator of `n(n²−1)/3`, so the closed form is exactly zero for every `n`. In `Double` it is zero to within one ulp rather than bit-exact, so compare it against a tolerance, not against `0.0`; [`dev_docs/STATISTICS_MEASUREMENTS.md`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/dev_docs/STATISTICS_MEASUREMENTS.md) has the sweep that bound comes from. And a quantised predictor (a bucketed index, an integer control value, a thresholded signal) is answered correctly: heavy ties with a real relationship still read high (a ten-block staircase reads **0.891**), while heavy ties with no relationship read ~0. Inputs whose `x` values are all distinct are unaffected, bit for bit, so every number elsewhere on this page is a tie-free case. Every other coefficient here refuses a constant outright: `pearson`, `spearman` and `kendallTauB` return NaN, and `distanceCorrelation` returns 0.0. ??? aside "Agents: xi values recorded before 2026-07-30" Recorded xi values on tied `x` from before 2026-07-30 are wrong, not merely different: x-ties then broke by input index, which scored how nearly `y` was a function of the order the samples arrived in. [`dev_docs/stdlib_behaviour_changes.md`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/dev_docs/stdlib_behaviour_changes.md) owns that history and the `chatterjeeXi` KDoc points at it. ## Measuring the null yourself There are no p-values in this family. That matters most for distance correlation, because dCor under genuine independence is **not** 0 at finite n: the estimator is biased upward, and the bias is large enough to swamp a real effect if you do not know its size. The `independent` row above reads 0.068 at n=400; shrink the sample and the bias grows fast, and by n=25 the null's 95th percentile is up at 0.466. So measure the null yourself. Re-pair `y` against `x` at random a few hundred times, and see where the number you actually observed falls: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/statistics_examples/null_distribution.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="820" padding="16"} :::static val n = 400 val x = DoubleArray(n) { it / (n - 1.0) * 2.0 - 1.0 } val rng = java.util.Random(7) val noise = DoubleArray(n) { rng.nextGaussian() } val y = DoubleArray(n) { (0.05 + abs(x[it])) * noise[it] } // the growing-spread panel again val observedDcor = StatsDependence.distanceCorrelation(x, y) val observedXi = StatsDependence.xi(x, y) // The null: break the pairing, keep both marginals. The observed 0.1934 is beyond every one of 400 random re-pairings (**0 / 400**), whose 95th percentile is 0.1262 and whose maximum is 0.1758. The dependence is real even though `pearson` reads −0.002. And in the same run xi reads 0.0263 against its own null's 95th percentile of 0.0520, with **76 / 400** re-pairings doing at least as well: xi has correctly declined to call this a functional relationship. The second figure gives you the shortcut for next time. Plotted against `1/√n` rather than `n`, the measured 95th percentile falls on a **straight line through the origin**, and the line's slope is about 2.5. Read the measured-against-predicted pairs off the bottom of the figure: 0.335/0.354 at n = 50 through 0.123/0.125 at n = 400, with the rule erring safely high at n = 25 (0.466 measured against 0.500 predicted). At n = 50 the threshold is around 0.34, so anything short of a strong relationship is invisible; distance correlation needs a few hundred samples before it can see a subtle one. ## Rolling: finding when the relationship starts A single coefficient over a whole recording answers the wrong question if the relationship comes and goes. `RollingDistanceCorrelation` maintains its row sums, grand sums and cross sums incrementally, so a `push` costs O(w) rather than the O(w²) a rebuild would (`correlations.kt:673#The maintained row sums, grand sums and cross sums are only ever`). `RollingXiCorrelation` makes no such promise. It recomputes `chatterjeeXi` over the window every time, at O(w log w) (`correlations.kt:917#have arrived. Copies the window out in arrival order first,`– `correlations.kt:928#val slot = (head + i) % windowSize`). That makes it exactly as trustworthy as the batch call and no faster. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/statistics_examples/rolling_regime.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="620" padding="16"} :::static val w = 80 val total = 600 val change = 300 val rng = java.util.Random(3) val dcor = RollingDistanceCorrelation(w) val xiRoll = RollingXiCorrelation(w) val xs = ArrayList() val ys = ArrayList() val dSeries = ArrayList() val xiSeries = ArrayList() val absR = ArrayList() for (i in 0 until total) { val xv = rng.nextGaussian() // Before `change`: two independent Gaussians. The pointwise 95th-percentile levels describe independent Gaussian windows, and the figure reports the first crossings for this seeded recording. Overlapping windows are correlated; these are not multiple-testing-adjusted change alarms, and their first crossings do not establish a general latency winner. Both settled dependence averages rise clearly after the change. Rolling `|pearson|` still swings across much the same range before and after it: a small-window absolute correlation has a positive noise floor, so reading it against zero would mislead. The last line of that figure cross-checks two different algorithms. `RollingDistanceCorrelation` never rebuilds a distance matrix (it only adds to and subtracts from maintained sums), while `StatsDependence.distanceCorrelation` materialises two full w×w matrices and double-centres them (`correlations.kt:419#matrices, which puts the practical ceiling at a few thousand`–`correlations.kt:499#val dcor = dcov / sqrt(dvarx * dvary)`). On the final window they agree to **5×10⁻¹⁵**. The KDoc warns that the maintained sums accumulate floating-point drift over a long run (`correlations.kt:674#recomputed, so a very long run accumulates floating-point drift`), and they do, though not far: over **200 000** pushes with a window of 64, the largest disagreement sampled against the batch call was **8.6×10⁻¹⁴**. `RollingDependenceTest` pins both bounds. ## Reshaping a distribution: `quantilewarp.kt` `AdaptiveQuantileWarp` does not measure anything: it fits a monotone 8-knot PCHIP curve from the measured quantiles of recent samples onto the quantiles of a target distribution, so a signal of the wrong shape becomes one of the right shape. The default target is `TargetDistributions.UnitNormal` (`quantilewarp.kt:94#val UnitNormal = QuantileFunction { p ->`), and the default eight probabilities are `0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.20, 0.50, 0.80, 0.95, 0.99`, which are **not symmetric** (`quantilewarp.kt:46#private val defaultQuantileWarpProbabilities = doubleArrayOf(`), so the fit spends more knots on the left tail than the right. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/statistics_examples/quantile_warp.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="820" padding="16"} :::static val rng = java.util.Random(5) val fit = DoubleArray(4000) { exp(rng.nextGaussian()) } // log-normal: violently right-skewed val held = DoubleArray(4000) { exp(rng.nextGaussian()) } // a second, disjoint draw val warp = AdaptiveQuantileWarp() // target: UnitNormal, 8 knots val state = warp.update(fit) val warped = held.map { state.evaluate(it) } val before = buildSummaryStats(held.toList()) val after = buildSummaryStats(warped) /* An independent oracle for the 8-knot fit: the *exact* warp onto a unit normal is Phi^-1(Fhat(v)), the inverse normal CDF of the empirical CDF of the fitting sample. Skewness goes from **11.68** to **0.0074**, excess kurtosis from **254.8** to **−0.170**, mean to −0.0024 and standard deviation to 1.0096. Eight knots and a PCHIP is enough to turn a log-normal into something you can treat as normal, and the first figure says how much is lost doing it: over the 2nd-to-98th percentile the 8-knot curve is within **0.047** of the exact `Φ⁻¹(F̂(v))` it is approximating. The left histogram in the same figure is the reason you would bother: with a maximum of 72.98 against a median of 0.98, the raw distribution is one spike and a tail, and no amount of binning makes it readable. Nothing in `quantilewarp.kt` computes that exact answer, so the oracle is built in the fence out of `inverseStandardNormalCdf` (`quantilewarp.kt:908#fun inverseStandardNormalCdf(p: Double): Double {`, itself accurate to six decimals: it returns 1.959964 at p=0.975 and −3.090232 at p=0.001) and a binary search over the sorted fitting sample. Three things to watch for: - **Outside the fitted range, `evaluate` extrapolates linearly from the endpoint tangent** (`quantilewarp.kt:183#tangent, with nothing clamping the result`), and for a compressed tail that slope is steep. On the fit above, whose lowest input knot is 0.038, `evaluate(0.0)` returns −3.75 and `evaluate(-1.0)` returns **−21.1**. Nothing clamps it. If your signal can leave the range you fitted on, clamp the input yourself. - **Successive states are smoothed, not replaced.** `smoothingAlpha` defaults to **0.20** (`quantilewarp.kt:146#val smoothingAlpha: Double = 0.20,`) and each `update` lerps the previous knots 20% of the way to the new ones (`quantilewarp.kt:357#lerp(previous.inputKnots[index], strictInputKnots[index], config.smoothingAlpha)`). Feed a signal whose median jumps from 0 to 10 and the median knot goes 0.009 → 2.016 → 3.608 → 4.879 → … → 9.310 after twelve updates, tracking `10·(1 − 0.20)ᵏ`: 0.690 remaining against a predicted 0.687. Convergence is geometric, so a step change takes a couple of dozen frames to follow. - **The knots are forced strictly increasing after smoothing** (`quantilewarp.kt:364#values = smoothedInputKnots,`), so the curve stays invertible even when the input degenerates; swept from −5 to 60 in steps of 0.01 the fitted curve above is strictly increasing throughout. `AdaptiveQuantileWarp` also keeps a history: `update` merges the batch you hand it with the last `historyFrames` batches (default **8**, `quantilewarp.kt:139#val historyFrames: Int = 8,`) before taking quantiles, so the knots are fitted on eight frames' worth of samples, not one. And the whole state packs into four `vec4`s for push constants. `applyToPushConstants` plus the matching GLSL include named by `FIELD_QUANTILE_WARP_INCLUDE_NAME` evaluate the identical curve on the GPU, and `Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp` (`quantilewarp.kt:553#fun Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp(`) closes that loop for you: it installs a runloop hook that drains a [shader field probe](field_probes.md), updates the warp and calls your `apply` callback with the new state. --- ## Choosing, in one paragraph Start with `distanceCorrelation`: it is the only one that is zero *only* under independence, so it is the right screen. Beat `2.5/√n` or you have found nothing. If it fires, ask what shape: `pearson` for a line, `spearman` or `kendallTauB` for monotone-but-curved, `xi` for "is `y` a function of `x`" including non-monotone ones. Hand `xi` its two arrays in the order you mean them, since it is the one coefficient here that answers a different question when you swap them. Reach for `micTicNaive` only for intuition, and never to compare against published MIC numbers. Above a few thousand samples, `kendallTauB` and `distanceCorrelation` are both O(n²) and `distanceCorrelation` also allocates two n×n matrices, so switch to `RollingDistanceCorrelation` or subsample. And if the problem turns out to be that the signal is the wrong shape rather than unrelated to anything, that is `quantilewarp.kt`.
